sn15.13:1.2: The same thirty monks from Pāvā visited the Buddha on another occasion when he was at Sāvatthī, occasioning the allowance for the robe-making ceremony after the rains residence ([pli-tv-kd7:1.1.1]()). | Pāvā, a town of the Mallas, was where Mahāvīra died, plunging the Jains into chaos. (The Jains, however, say this was another Pāvā east of Nāḷandā.) Perhaps because of this, Pāvā became associated with especially ascetic monks such as those in this discourse: Mahākassapa heard the news of the Buddha’s passing at Pāvā; and sixty monks from Pāvā allied with monks of “Avanti and the south” arguing for strict Vinaya in the Second Council ([pli-tv-kd22:1.7.11.1]()).
sn15.13:1.4: “Living in the wilderness” means rejecting life in settled monasteries. | “Eating only almsfood” means rejecting invitations for meals in people’s houses, or organized meals served in the monastery, taking only what is received in the village. | “Wearing rag robes” means rejecting robes made from new cloth, and making robes only from discarded cloth, cleaned and patched together. | “Owning just three robes” means rejecting extra robes such as a bathing cloth, and wearing only the three main robes of a mendicant: the “lower robe” or “sarong” (_antarāvāsaka_); the “upper robe” (_uttarasaṅga_); and the double-layered “outer robe” or “cloak” (_saṅghāṭi_).
sn15.13:2.3: The similes in this chapter are powerful, but this is especially brutal.
sn15.13:3.12: I can’t help feeling that something stronger is required here for paradarika, i.e rape. But I can’t find any contexts that clarify whether consent was an issue in this crime.
